sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Lesesalen is a Mastodon client that shows you the book posts and nothing else. Five kinds of book post, five distinct looks, laid out as a reading room rather than a microblogging timeline.

BookWyrm has no public API, but it federates. Every BookWyrm post reaches your Mastodon home timeline as a plain note. The trouble is that Mastodon discards the rich fields: the rating, the review title, the quoted passage, how far into the book the reader is, and the link to the book are all custom ActivityPub properties Mastodon has no column for.

sections.heading: Why a server exists
paragraphs: The origin object is still public and addressable. Fetch it with Accept: application/activity+json and you get the whole thing back — type, rating, title, quote, position and the link to the edition.

The browser cannot do this itself, because BookWyrm instances do not send CORS headers for ActivityPub fetches. That single fact is the entire reason a server exists in this project. It does three things: it looks up what software an instance runs, it re-fetches the origin object, and it caches bibliographic data and cover images.

sections.heading: What it deliberately is not
paragraphs: You see a post because you follow that account, or because someone you follow boosted it. Same as Mastodon. Nothing more.

So there is no crawler. Lesesalen does not walk the fediverse collecting BookWyrm posts into a database. Those posts are public, but public is not the same as consenting to be aggregated, indexed and re-served by a third party the author never heard of. A BookWyrm user posting a review to their followers did not sign up to be in somebody's corpus.
For the same reason there is no logged-out feed and no discovery surface. A stranger arriving here sees an explainer and some invented samples, not other people's reading.

The one exception is clicking an author and seeing their posts. That is an ordinary client affordance: it goes through your own instance with your own token, and it shows exactly what Mastodon would show you.

sections.heading: Replies
paragraphs: You can reply, favourite and boost through the Mastodon API. A reply becomes an ordinary Mastodon post — not a BookWyrm comment. Mastodon cannot mint BookWyrm objects, and we would rather say so once too often than once too rarely.

sections.heading: Contact
paragraphs: Lesesalen fetches from instances we do not own, and tries to be a polite guest: one request per second per domain, an honest User-Agent, and we honour 429 and Retry-After. If it is nonetheless a nuisance, get in touch and we will fix it.

privacy.title: Privacy

points.detail: The server has no user table. There is no login on the server side at all.
Your credentials stay in your browser and go only to your own instance.
Your social graph is never transmitted to the server. Only bare domain names are, in batches, to answer the question "is this instance BookWyrm".
Post content passes through memory and is discarded. A restart empties everything, which is correct.

points.term: No analytics, no cookies, no third-party anything
points.detail: No tracking, no CDN, no external scripts or fonts.

kept: Which fediverse instances run BookWyrm. That is infrastructure, not personal information, and one lookup serves everybody.
Bibliographic data and cover images for books that have been seen: title, authors, page count, ISBN and the link to BookWyrm. A book edition is not anyone's personal information.

Covers are downloaded once, when a book is first cached, and then served from here. So your IP never reaches the instance that owns the image, and because the fetch happens at cache time rather than per view, the server learns nothing about who looked at what.
privacy.caveat: The endpoint that fetches origin objects receives the URIs of the posts being viewed. So the server transiently sees which posts someone is reading. They are not logged, not stored and not associated with any identity, and the cache is shared so requests are not attributable to a person. But it is not nothing, and it belongs here rather than glossed over.
privacy.rights: There is no export feature and no delete feature, because there is nothing to export and nothing to delete. To remove your login, log out: the token is revoked at your instance first, then cleared from the browser.
